between Segal-Bargmann spaces for the generalized and classical cases. Furthermore, 
it has been demonstrated that the generalized transformation preserves the positive definite 
hermitian property. Additionally, calculations involving the norm and inner product 
in the Segal-Bargmann space, formulated via the generalized transformation, were 
carried out and found to align with their corresponding expressions in the classical 
instance. Lastly, exploration of the generalized transformation's connection to 
Clifford analysis was also initiated.

We establish that a class of Gaussian fields possess the property that the expectation of a functional of the field's trajectory conditioned on its values at distinct spatial points is equal to the expectation of the same functional for a field that is conditioned on those points and then averaged over all possible realizations of the relevant secondary field. In the specific context of Gaussian fields, this relationship provides a justification for the strategy of first conditioning the field and then taking the expectation over all possible secondary fields, thereby allowing us to construct non-trivial examples of fields for which the secondary field may be specified non-randomly. As a consequence, this approach can be employed to derive the exact distribution of the path of a Bessel process upon conditioning on its initial values, thereby synthesizing a random variable whose squared magnitude is exponentially distributed with parameter one, along with an independent uniform variable on the interval $[0,1)$. Similarly, we utilize our method to derive the joint distribution of the times of entry and exit for Brownian motion in a specific region shaped like an elongated ellipse. Finally, by conditioning on the field's values at two distinct points, we are also able to establish that the distribution of the inverse of a multiple independent and identically distributed random variable is a generalized inverse Gaussian distribution, thereby synthesizing a random variable whose squared magnitude is exponentially distributed with parameter one and a variable whose distribution is a mixture of the variables 1/\sqrt(t) and 1/\sqrt(1-t) with coefficients 1 and

This research demonstrates that in the context of a ground-and-sky sensor network, tight ground coverage enables detection of falling objects, while simultaneous sky coverage facilitates recognition of airborne entities. Developed is an efficient approach for forming connections between sensors located on the ground and sensors floating above, without requiring the precise calculation of locations or channels to achieve this goal. Our innovative method achieves feasible and efficient object tracking by leveraging a ground network with optimal ground coverage and an adaptable sky network that adjusts to changing sensor relationships in real-time. Valuable research results are also yielded through the analysis of a problem model, including an algorithm with constant ratio optimization and a theoretical bound on communication cost. Simulation outcomes confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving seamless communication between ground and sky sensors, resulting in seamless object tracking across both spaces.

The ultimate goal of neutrino research, achieving 100% flavor conservation, still remains unsolved. We propose a pioneering deep-earth neutrino experiment designed to measure oscillations over extremely long distances. Featuring an uncompromising high-precision design, the project aims to and refine our understanding of neutrino physics. Detailed geological assessments at potential site options in South Africa and North Africa are currently underway. This study outlines the reasons behind choosing a deep-earth location, an overview of anticipated conditions, target characteristics, and experimental details, and finally, suggests the advantages and development opportunities presented by such an innovative project.

A key challenge in identifying the top quark's decay products lies in distinguishing tagged top quarks from tagged W bosons. The underlying physics question revolves around identifying the tagged top quark signal within a complex mixture of signal and background events. To address this, we developed enhanced top tagging algorithms built on a regression-based approach. We introduced new features specifically designed for top tagging, including algebraic products and categorization techniques based on subassemblies. Furthermore, we utilized the Shapley Value technique to allocate the responsibility of tag efficiency to various decision-making components. We optimized our algorithms against both tagged W bosons and untagged jets with an emphasis on robustness, and we believe these algorithms can be valuable tools in many scenarios where top tagging is applied, especially in regions dominated by tagged W bosons.

This document formalizes advanced multi-level coordinated view-only (VO) 
relationships applicable to multiple domains such as coordination, 
communication, collaboration, and control, which involve various entities 
like humans or robots, within a shared environment or virtual space. VO 
encompasses a broad spectrum of interactions ranging from coordination and 
communication to the more intricate aspects of robot collaboration and 
control. The document systematically breaks down and formalizes the VO 
concept along with its subcategories to enhance understanding and identification 
when implementing advanced VO mechanisms. Furthermore, it outlines a strategy 
for expanding and customizing VO to suit diverse scenarios within multiple 
contexts.

To accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) training, techniques such as importance sampling, off-policy learning, and experience replay have been utilized. While experience replay proves particularly beneficial in deep RL, its standard implementation can sometimes hinder training by emphasizing rare events over common ones. This is because the approach measures policy performance based on the expected value, which can lead to increased variance and hinder the learning process. To address this shortcoming, a new variance-reducing approach to experience replay has been proposed, which utilizes a more stable estimate of the task reward. By minimizing variance in reward estimates, the proposed method enhances the efficiency of off-policy RL algorithms and promotes policy enhancements. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this novel approach not only accelerates RL training but also facilitates policy improvements compared to existing methods, while showcasing robustness across a range of RL and transfer learning scenarios.

Two new transformation techniques have been proposed recently: a generalized version of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula. Both methods aim to tackle the challenges in Gaussian integrations involving odd operators with positive definite metrics in both bosonic and fermionic systems. This work focuses on comparing these two methods, applying them to derive an alternative form of the superbosonization formula that is more efficient and encompasses systems with Grassmann codomain. Additionally, it showcases specific applications where these transformations result in similar and equivalent forms in bosonic systems.

Our goal with end-to-end spatiotemporal predictive learning using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is panning down on a particular approach that has recently generated significant interest. However, the existing RNN-based models, including our recently proposed Model Transformer for Spatiotemporal prediction with Recurrent structure (MeTS-R), tend to focus on overall motion patterns rather than breaking down features by part. This limits their ability to effectively capture and utilize detailed motion information in predictive learning settings. In an effort to improve our comprehension and address this shortcoming, we introduce a variation of the MeTS-R model, known as MoDeRNN, which integrates a decoupled motion descriptor for capturing more precise representations of motions across multiple scales. Our proposed approach is thoroughly evaluated in a comprehensive series of experiments, and the results demonstrate the potential of this idea to contribute to the advancement of end-to-end spatiotemporal predictive learning using RNNs.

This research focuses on addressing memory safety issues in the next-generation web platform, particularly when interacting with web content written in WebAssembly. Our investigation aims to compare memory safety features in various languages and APIs, culminating in an experimental framework that uses JavaScript to safely manage memory in WebAssembly applications alongside Rust's existing memory management. The introduction of a new abstract data type in JavaScript enables the creation of a lifetime-based approach to memory safety, complemented by performance-correct exception points. These exceptions points, implemented in both Rust and JavaScript, allow for predictable memory handling by combining the benefits of monomorphic (Rust) and polymorphic (JavaScript) type checks. The paper outlines memory abstraction, lifetime rules, and exception point guidelines, accompanied by performance measurements and case studies. The proposed approach was successfully prototyped and tested in the Uno runtime environment.

The investigation of neutrinoless double-beta decay provides crucial information about the properties of neutrinos, including the mass of the electron neutrino. This study examines the signature of neutrinoless double-beta decay at future colliders, focusing on the specific case of $e^+e^-\rightarrow eeJJ$. By analyzing this process, researchers can extract the value of the $NN$ coupling constant associated with with Majorana fermion pairs. Interference between Majorana states, caused by the $NN\tilde{\nu}\tilde{\nu}$ vertex, may lead to a measurable signal, even if neutrinos have non-zero masses. As a result, a future $100\text{ fb}^{-1}$ electron-positron collider operating at $10\,\text{GeV}$ could establish the existence of this coupling at a confidence level of $5.8\,\sigma$, assuming Majorana neutrino masses of up to $5\,\text{eV}$. This research also indicates that the $NN$ coupling constant is correlated with the mass of the Higgs boson in the form of $m_{H}/\sqrt{\lambda_{NN}}$.

Channel decoding methodology, specifically for polar codes, tends to categorize decoding strategies into SP and BP categories. While successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding falls into the BP category. This paper introduces a novel approach called polar subcode (PS) decoding, also classified under the BP category, yet features an inherently set-inclusive decoding list with restricted error propagation, ultimately resulting in reduced list sizes compared to SCL. Furthermore, PS decoding can be viewed as a specialized GC decoding method where submatrices of the transition probability matrix are utilized, enabling efficient parallel processing through parallel computation systems. Under the assumption of an asymptotically optimal PS decoder, we derive the belief propagation (BP) decoding error probability and provide practical decoding rules. Results show that PS decoding can achieve a 30% reduction in list size over SCL decoding and outperforms it in terms of BP decoding error probability, especially at low SNR values. This new decoding method offers enhanced computational efficiency, decreased memory requirements, and lower latency, making it suitable for implementation on distributed computing systems.

Images from space telescopes often get distorted by the telescope's optical issue, but we can use various techniques to rectify this. Normally, images are corrected through a process called deconvolution, but some galaxies have objects that appear out of focus due to a specific issue with the Hubble Space Telescope's lens. These particular galaxies have multiple images that become more sharp when their shapes are known and used to correct for the lens's effect, but combining them requires a precise calculation to produce a clear image. This calculation, known as a demagnification, is typically given for each position but varies according to direction, making it challenging to correct the distortion in the image. This issue is addressed with a new method that uses a parameterised expression to describe the lens's effect with varying position, allowing for overall correction of the image's distortion. Demagnification values obtained from the analysis are provided for different positions in the Hubble Space Telescope's field of view, allowing for a standard correction procedure for the lens's effect. This correction is then demonstrated to improve the deconvolution process of the images by reducing discontinuities and improving the accuracy of the results.

Building upon previous research that modeled the properties of amorphous materials, we have developed a continuous crack-growth theory for brittle materials. Focusing on the persistence of crack growth resistance beyond its initial threshold, we have identified essential elements of the material's fabric, such as local stress concentrations and Crack-Stop Layer formation. Our findings reveal that a crack's resistance indeed diminishes without this layer. Furthermore, we have demonstrated how the presence of this layer influences the fundamental fracture parameters, including energy release rates and crack tip pressures. Notably, we have discovered that a small layer can profoundly lower a material's overall fracture toughness, often by an order of magnitude. Our approach accommodates various crack geometries and initial angles, and we discuss how realistic material micromechanics might look like based on our results.

Building on recent findings of Dub\'e and Gnutzmann--Schmidt related to multiple SLE tapes, we provide a novel demonstration of the existence of a finite volume domain wall conformal field theory that corresponds to the limit of the O(n) model on the lattice as n approaches 0. Additionally, we show that the primary correlation function in this theory exhibits a certain non-local invertible operator derivative, a property that gives rise to an embedded conformal field theory equivalent to the "multiple join" CFT of multiple SLE tapes. We also establish that the dual CFT of Dub\'e--Gnutzmann--Schmidt corresponds to the domain wall version of the "multiple join" CFT. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these CFTs are associated with the domain wall version of the O(n) model on the lattice as n approaches 0. Also, by relating them to the solvable O(n)-symmetric Gaussian free field on the plane, we arrive at an equivalent interpretation of the findings of Gerasimchuk about the spontaneous magnetization in the lattice Gaussian free field. Also, by using Schaeffer's formula, we prove (along with recent results of Chhaya--Rangamani--Scheel) that the vorticity of Schr\"odinger eigenfunctions on the plane, as studied by Craig-Major, has at most a C(3/2, l) regularity for small l.

This research investigates the existence and characteristics of solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations in a periodic setting, focusing on the behavior of solutions in time. By employing a specific, simple test function, whose properties are independent of the viscosity parameter, we assess the existence of solutions and derive bounds on the growth of the solution. Importantly, this approach does not rely on a small initial condition or a specific viscosity parameter value. As a byproduct of this method, we demonstrate that solutions to the 3D periodic Navier-Stokes equations with certain initial conditions are stable, and their behavior can be described in terms of the viscosity parameter. Additionally, we show that solutions to the 3D periodic Navier-Stokes equations with very large initial conditions may ultimately become unstable and enter a chaotic state, which is characterized by highly fluctuating velocities, regardless of the viscosity parameter value.

We've developed an efficient verification method to ensure the correct implementation of quantum gate calculations, capable of detecting any type of error. Our approach combines the principles of hash functions and verifies quantum gate calculations using classical linear-time operations, despite the exponential complexity of some quantum operations. Importantly, this verification method doesn't disrupt the underlying quantum calculations and can operate without interfering with the state of the quantum computer. This allows the verification process to run concurrently with the quantum calculations. Our experimental findings validate the theoretical efficiency of this verification method and demonstrate its practical scalability by successfully verifying a series of combined quantum gate calculations that simulate complex quantum algebra operations like the Jordan-Wigner transformation for spin systems and linear optical cloning for multiple qubit states.

A growing number of applications rely on blockchain technology, but its full potential remains underutilized due to infrequent transactions. Internet of Things (IoT) transactions occur at a high frequency, which poses challenges for batch verification. This research presents a novel blockchain framework tailored to IoT transactions, incorporating features of BlockChain Customized to IoT (BC-IOIT), intelligent contracts, and oracle services. Our framework supports diverse IoT transactions and integrates three modules: smart contract creation, transaction validation, and IoT data integration. Utilizing BC-IOIT, the framework achieves increased throughput and efficiency. Our proposed approach successfully demonstrates this concept in a real-world setting, such as a food distribution supply chain.

We explore the application of a technique called NeRF, normally used in computer graphics, to model and simulate cell morphology. Our approach develops an unsupervised method to use cell contour images at different stages to create 3D representations of cell forms. By extending NeRF to model complex, non-spherical shapes, we were able to create accurate, continuous topological maps of cell surfaces from multiple views. Our approach proven effective on a comprehensive dataset of cat kidney cells, outperformed previous methods and enabled the creation of detailed, volumetric models from new, unseen images.

In the digital age, information technologyAccessibility has made significant strides, but there are still gaps in understanding user needs, particularly concerning accessibility practices across countries. This study investigates the importance of computer accessibility and digital media practice in India, where this research focuses, and its relevance to the needs of visually impaired and visually impaired-like users. It aims to offer practical solutions toward enhancing computer accessibility in India, offering concrete methods that can be implemented in everyday life as well as contributing to the broader global discussion on computer accessibility.

Recently introduced autoregressive language models have achieved remarkable success in various language tasks, but they are constrained by their predictive nature, which forces them to rely on earlier information when predicting later inputs. This limitation is alleviated with the revised XLNet, a generalized autoregressive pretraining model, which can perform predictive tasks in both forward and reverse directions. This enhanced model enables the use of a broader range of self-attention patterns, including those that focus on earlier tokens when predicting later ones, thus overcoming the limitations of existing autoregressive models. Experimental results demonstrate XLNet's superiority over other cutting-edge models, including RoBERTa and BERT, on a range of tasks, including text classification, question answering, and sentence construction.

We have developed computational models designed to analyze the effects of stellar activity on spectroscopic analysis in exoplanet research. We have applied these models to study how stellar activity impacts transit depth and transmission spectroscopy across various planetary scenarios and atmospheric compositions. We have investigated the reliability of high-resolution spectroscopy in minimizing these effects and found that this technique can significantly alleviate contamination, reducing by half the number of planets needed to confirm the exoplanet hypothesis through transmission spectroscopy. Our models also reveal that as resolution decreases, models that assume clear skies become increasingly inaccurate, while models that account for water absorption remain relatively accurate across a range of resolutions. We propose a multi-step approach to identify planets with the most suitable conditions for transit spectroscopy and spectroscopic binarity detection, involving both observational and computational phases, to enhance our chances of detecting life in exoplanets.

We develop a method for constructing conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces that feature singularities, building upon previous approaches for complete surfaces. The key innovation involves using anomalous net metrics, which have curvatures that diverge but meet specified criteria at singular points. Through a detailed calculation of the anomalous degree in the conformal framework, and consideration of a key topological constraint, we determine the conditions necessary for existence. Subsequently, under the assumption of their existence, we demonstrate the existence of a unique solution for the metric and establish its dependence on previously chosen metrics at singular points. Furthermore, we establish the metrics' smoothness, excluding a set of lower dimension, and establish its relationship with the original metric. Lastly, we establish the metrics' unique representation up to scaling.

This study delves into the movement patterns of a novel, 27-do-freedom robotic centipede designed to mimic the water-gaiting strategies employed by the Anelaspis semi-aquatic centipede. To achieve this, we took an interdisciplinary approach, combining insights from biologically inspired robotics and the characteristics of semi-aquatic centipede locomotion. Focusing on the key factors that control water-gaiting dynamics in legged locomotors, we utilized Lagrangian mechanics to develop a comprehensive mathematical framework. Our research revealed that the 27-do-freedom robotic system can be reduced to an integrable nonlinear ODE system, with our theoretical predictions matching the actual experimental results of the robotic centipede. Additionally, we demonstrated that our inspiration from Anelaspis's water-gain movement led to a substantial enhancement in the robot's mobility and stability when moving on a water-surface, resulting in an increase of 3 times more mobility when compared to other state-of-the-art legged locomotors on a water-surface.

The ultimate goal of this project is to create an openly accessible, high-performance computing code that can simulate tsunami behavior and its effects on local areas in the event of an asteroid impact that triggers the Earth's dispersive wave behavior. To achieve this goal, we are developing a flexible modeling approach utilizing the finite element method in the ElmerICE code, which is specifically designed for fluid dynamics and wave propagation in the solid Earth's context, and is already utilized by researchers in the fields of seismology and tsunami modeling. This code will be further developed by adjusting multiple factors that influence its run time, including the size of the asteroid and the event's epicenter distance, and the level of local coastal detail for more accurate sub-meter predictions. This optimization strategy, grounded in computational science principles, will allow us to identify the most effective factors to adjust for specific scenarios, ultimately resulting in an adaptive simulation tool that can be utilized by researchers in the fields of asteroid impact, seismology, and tsunami modeling to study various scenarios, and their interactions within the field of astropaleontology.

Recent observations from the ALMA and ATLAS$^3d'$^+$ survey have identified a subset of galaxies consisting mainly of late-stage star-forming galaxies, both luminous and dim in infrared spectra, with elevated stellar masses. These galaxies show relatively low molecular gas reserves and star-forming rates. A new dataset from the JWST is used to investigate the differences between these bright and dim galaxies within the same infrared brightness of about $L_{TIR} = 4 \times 10^{10} M_{sun} yr^{-1}$. It has been observed that galaxies with low optical brightness but high infrared brightness exhibit lower dust temperatures, decreased neon emission, and lower ionized gas reserves. These characteristics suggest that these galaxies are heavily obscured with large amounts of dust, restricting the visibility of their optical and neon emissions. By comparing these characteristics to those obtained by the JWST, early ARCoLS spectra are able to identify the extensive extinction effects present in these dim galaxies, leading to increased star formation efficiencies. A simulation indicates that if the extinction effects were removed, these galaxies would primarily consist of older stellar populations, indicating that these galaxies are nearing the end of their star-forming periods, powered by gas compression from nearby galaxies, fueling their final stages of star formation. A large number of such events are predicted to contribute to the formation of quenching or post-starburst galaxies, could explain a significant portion of (sub)millimeter-selected galaxies' prolonged star-forming periods

This research focuses on understanding the fundamental aspects of seven-dimensional gravity, characterized by the interaction of two distinct forms of gravity, and a dual relationship with a physically significant topological field, reminiscent of Chern-Simons gravity in lower dimensions. By implementing a straightforward mathematical approach, we derive solutions that satisfy the Einstein equations, leveraging an existing theorem that simplifies this task. Our results include two categories of solutions: those that exhibit pure topological properties with vanishing curvature, and others with measurable curvature, comparible to the Schwarzschild model in higher dimensions. Additionally, we extend the fundamentals of gravity theory by introducing a new field, denoted as $\mathcal{F}_{R_{3}}$, which defines the curvature based on an intrinsic spin connection and a specific connection variable. This extension has the practical implication of enabling the coupling of the gravity field, represented by $\mathcal{F}_{7}$, with the newly introduced field $\mathcal{F}_{R_{3}}$.

This work extends our investigation into a specific numerical model, previously developed to simulate dusty planetary formation in a planetary disk. Previously, we analyzed a three-dimensional version of the model with a simplified, constant width geometry. This time, we'll explore a two-dimensional version, modeled using the Heidrich-Minkovich algorithm, in a complex, winding shape. Our study will focus on how particle masses influence the simulation, in a environment where gas and dust interact, with dust particles behaving like solid particles. We've discovered that when particle masses are evenly distributed, the simulation behaves as expected, with particles converging on a regular pattern. However, when we varied the ratio of gas to solid viscosity, the simulation exhibited periodic patterns. In a follow-up study, we investigated this behavior and found that this phenomenon is not unique to this particular setup, but can also occur with large numbers of particles, under specific geometric and numerical conditions.

Research indicates that East African precipitation is mainly influenced by ENSO cycles, specifically El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na events.  These cycles impact the Indian Ocean's atmospheric circulation in reverse ways, resulting in contrasting low and high seasonal precipitation in the region, including fluctuations in downpours and boosting droughts.  A new study has linked ENSO types to the occurrence of heavy rainfall and severe droughts in the region.  By analyzing long-term data on downpours and general precipitation from 1970-2018, the research shows that El Ni\~no events lead to elevated infra-red and very heavy precipitation, whereas La Ni\~na events cause decreased infra-red rainfall and elevated droughts.  These findings were confirmed by modeling past climates, specifically the last 400 years, and show that East Africa's rainfall anomalies follow the ENSO cycle in a predictable pattern.

To examine the dynamic light scattering (DLS) response of bending modulated planar epoxy films during non-affine elastic deformation, a laboratory-based experimental approach was developed.  The epoxy film, initially intact, was subjected to a non-affine regime of large strains via a periodic 3D-bent silicon rib, and this multi-scale technique led to a continuous strain monitoring method.  The intensity variation observed in the light scattering signal was found to be in perfect sync with the modulus loss curve obtained through nanoindentation, and this correlation was also similar to that reported in literature for polymers.  In contrast to affine behavior, this observed light scattering response appears to be an effective method for detecting non-affine elastic deformation in solids, and combining this approach with light scattering may offer a new way to analyze complex materials.

This research explores the effects of environmental toxicity and a phenomenon called behavioural change on a single species, taking into account individual development and a new model for behavioural adjustment. We established a single-species population model with discrete age categories and introduced a behaviour switch model, defining it as the process by which an individual's consciousness shifts from physical well-being to perceived quality of life. Combining this with an existing model, we developed a comprehensive mathematical framework, represented by a nonhomogeneous linear differential equation with matrices, and identified specific criteria for long-term population survival. We also used numerical methods to simulate real-life scenarios, presenting our findings in intuitive graphical formats.

First-order ensembles of certain very weak logics incorporating contraction have specific decidability characteristics due to an effective method for eliminating negative aspects from their formulas, leading to finite representation of their satisfiable models in canonical matrices. This same mechanism also makes certain second-order ensembles of these logics with an ensemble quantifier feasible. We introduce a new first-order ensemble that includes contraction and a form of hypersequent, is equivalent to the incidence calculus, and is denoted as LINC. We demonstrate that the subset of formulas that can be proved using an ensemble is decidable within that ensemble, for both the incidence relation and other general hypersequents. This makes all incidence calculi that can be represented using an ensemble decidable, in contrast to other similar logics. We also introduce an ensemble that can be represented using an ensemble, has a feasible two-way feasible method, and is equivalent to the generalized Kripke semantics for classical logic once an ensemble-based feasibility boundary is applied. This ensemble represents "all-encompassing" classical logic, is feasible to determine if its ensemble-based proofs are valid, and allows for a boundary-based feasibility evaluation of its generalizability.

Research indicates that neural network feature representations often generalize better when embedded in lower-dimensional spaces with non-Euclidean structures. This paper introduces HyperExpan, an innovative algorithm for expanding neural network classifications by generating new decision boundaries using hyperbolic representation learning. By adapting hyperbolic learning to neural network expansion, HyperExpan efficiently learns from existing models, achieving improved accuracy and reduced training time compared to conventional methods. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate HyperExpan's superiority over existing approaches.

The effect of electric fields on molecular interactions has been the focus of ongoing research in theoretical chemistry. Most studies have been centered on the response of individual molecules to electric fields, but there's still a knowledge gap when it comes to understanding the collective response of molecular pairs to a uniform electric field. A recent study used a high-performance, mathematically robust method to calculate the energy distribution of molecular pairs in response to electric fields, and it assessed the accuracy of these calculations by comparing them to accurate wavefunction calculations. The study used a standardized set of molecules and a standardized test case to evaluate the performance of these calculations as part of a larger effort to create a chemically diverse database of molecular interactions. The study found that the collective response of molecular pairs to electric fields is composed of two main components: the interaction between the molecules and the electric field, and the interaction between the molecules and each other. The study identified a group of energy patterns that contributed to the collective response and used a high-level mathematical model to separate the contributions of electric field-molecule and molecule-molecule interactions to the energy of these patterns. The study found that the effect of molecule-molecule interactions on these patterns was significantly reduced as the strength of the electric field increased, and it used this information to create a method for automatically separating the contributions of electric field-molecule and molecule-molecule interactions to the energy of molecular interactions in complex systems. The study showed that this separation of energy components is crucial for understanding the collective response of molecular pairs

The advent of Industry 4.0 has accelerated automation, leading to significant job job losses and heightened concerns about job instability. Despite the emergence of machine learning-based algorithms for scheduling, very few studies have explored the unique characteristics of service and construction sectors' job schedules. These environments are characterized by an inherent lack of data consistency due to tasks' inherently high levels of ambiguity. Ambiguity refers to the lack of job data standardization, making it a significant obstacle to leveraging machine learning algorithms in these sectors. The objective of this study is to demonstrate a novel method for addressing the challenges posed by ambiguity in Industry 4.0 scheduling, with particular emphasis on the implementation of non-deterministic ambiguity modeling. This method incorporates three components: non-deterministic ambiguity modeling, stochastic indexing, and quantized indexing techniques, which are combined to produce a ground-truth index for effective dispatching, thereby increasing the efficiency of dispatching tasks. The proposed method was tested using data from the Service4All dataset, with the results showcasing its utility and superiority in comparative experiments. Notably, the method achieved a 100% success rate and significantly outperformed existing methods by a remarkable 836.68%, while also reducing the computational time required to process the data compared to non-quantized methods.

This paper introduces a novel approach for evaluating the reliability of complex systems, crucial for critical cyber-physical systems that require dependable real-time performance. We use a logic system called STL (State Transition Logic), which defines system reliability based on desired real-time behaviors, and within this framework, we identify and distinguish robustness from two distinct concepts, endurance and reliability. Aiming to minimize resource consumption and enhance efficiency, we employ non-exhaustive verification methods to verify these properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology through a case study on the controller of a mecha system.

A novel approach for identifying substances via network vibrations is suggested, where specifically, U-net-inspired encoder-decoder architectures were applied to time series data captured by accelerometers. The data was initially pre-processed via PCA to reduce dimensionality. The encoding layer within the network was modified to account for systematic patterns in time series data. The newly formulated method was tested using Synthetic Data, where varying Factors were employed to simulate background noise and analyze data variability. The model's capacity to differentiate between data variability and factors affecting encoding was assessed, and it was found that incorporating temporal encoding yielded more precise substance identification results. Furthermore, employing RFE-EL onto time series data increased the diversity of substances that can be identified in cross-validation, effectively mitigating overfitting. It is envisioned that this technique will facilitate the search for occult substances in various applications.

We consider a nonlinear diffusion equation on complete, non-compact manifolds. By assuming the diffusion coefficient meets specific requirements and the initial data has limited growth, we demonstrate that the equation generates smooth solutions for all time, even on expansive manifolds. Furthermore, precise estimates of the solution's derivatives are derived, providing quantitative measures of the solution's smoothness and its sensitivity to initial conditions and diffusion parameters.

Researchers analyzing 20 GHz data from the TIFR GMRT Sky Survey found that by stacking, they could characterize and measure characteristics of vast numbers of galactic radio sources at the same time.  By examining 1,126 sources over 20 mJy/beam in 0.05 square degrees, they studied how various properties like flux density, spectral index and angular size of sources change with resolution.  They found through their analysis that galactic radio sources follow a trend of n=2 in relation to resolution.  Also, sources exhibiting narrow radio dimensions are predominantly categorized as radio sources of the compact Galactic halo while those with wider dimensions are either part of the CGH or young sources that have recently exploded.  Further K-corrections observation also revealed that extragalactic sources are more massive and brighter than galactic radio sources.  Also, relationships observed between flux density and angular size in galactic and extragalactic sources are similar.  Also, relationships observed between flux density and angular size in galactic and extragalactic sources showed minimal discrepancy.

We introduce the abstract version of the Concealed Markov Model, an extension of
probabilistic nets, and establish a high-level characterization of Concealed
Markov Models using the $\mathit{HPF}_\omega$ monad. This study offers a detailed
analysis of the effectiveness of an approach that quantifies information flow in
complex systems, such as those based on Markov models or probabilistic nets, in
a concise top-down manner. By focusing on their underlying data structures,
we define their operational behavior and establish their place within a broader
category of probabilistic programs. Your approach will be illustrated through
the application of these concepts to a real-world scenario: a discussion thread
where users may share sensitive information. Your analysis will determine the
probability that a third-party entity might discover confidential data, and
reveal the underlying structure of the information flow that leads to this
occurrence.

This paper develops a statistical concept of nonlocality, grounded in a novel
pattern-coherent measure, which assesses both spatially diffuse structuring
influences and the emergence of patterns themselves. Using the central concept
of dynamically consistent patterns, initially explored with examples, the research
establishes that nonlocality increases as patterns become more dispersed and
less coherent. It demonstrates the nonlocality measure's symmetry, finite values,
and connection to entropy. This statistical concept of nonlocality is applicable
to various spatiotemporal patterns and can be utilized across different fields.

We introduce an advanced scattering-based model, Flexible Scattering Phenomenology (FSP), built upon the Wilsonian effective action framework. It integrates all relevant higher-order corrections into a single, unified approach. FSP offers several key benefits, including the decoupling of theoretical and phenomenological calculations and the versatility to include or exclude specific higher-order terms as needed. We demonstrate the practical application of the FSP formalism through two benchmark scenarios, dark matter annihilation in fixed mediation channels and in fixed cross-section models. The introduction of the FSP formalism paves the way for more accurate and precise event-level simulations that can be used in concurrent phenomenological studies to determine the viability of specific models.

This paper presents the electromagnetic theory of a blackbody that accounts for both blackbody and Casimir radiation. It also develops the thermodynamic functions for its states, with an emphasis on establishing Einstein's Planck distribution as the correct thermodynamic equilibrium state within this framework. Furthermore, the paper establishes Boltzmann's distribution, derived from the Lagrange multipliers of the grand canonical ensemble, as the correct state for systems in thermodynamic equilibrium. Additionally, the paper investigates the total entropy of both Casimir and blackbody radiation to verify the third law of thermodynamics. Lastly, the paper examines total entropy behavior over a periodic process to verify the second law of thermodynamics.

Research has been conducted to assess the impact of losing location tracking privacy due to an attacker's prior knowledge of location history. To measure location tracking privacy, the L\'eprevost metric can be employed, which yields a privacy score based on the change of a prior probability distribution after acquiring new information. However, conventional analysis methods under unconditional priors may not be effective given that initial location information often provides significant insight. Therefore, a more suitable approach involves utilizing conditional priors that incorporate this initial information and reflecting it in the privacy score. Moreover, our research demonstrates that a conditional prior based on an historian's knowledge of location history can be modeled as a Markov mixture, which enables derivation of the posterior distribution and the computation of the revised L\'eprevost metric. It has been found that location tracking privacy is determined by the minimum eigenvalue of the posterior covariance matrix and the maximum angle between the posterior and prior normal distributions. Additionally, our research provides a privacy-computation efficiency chart for evaluating L\'eprevost metrics with conditional priors and illustrates that an attacker's location history length impacts privacy to an eighth power.

A highly precise and efficient method for localizing 3D point clouds in saturated environments has been developed using deep learning and norm-based spatial transformation. The algorithm begins by mapping 3D data onto 2D norm-space vision using Normal Distribution Transform, thus utilizing the existing extensive image databases to derive informative feature extracts. These refined features are subsequently combined using a multi-layered transformer architecture, which encodes spatial layout information and synergizes cues from depth sensors and gyroscope sensors. The resulting model achieves consistent and precise real-time position estimation with minimal latency, enabling seamless interaction between humans and robots equipped with depth sensors, capturing environment feature extracts via depth inference. Evaluation on a self-built dataset revealed the algorithm surpasses state-of-the-art methods globally in terms of position accuracy and latency.

A key objective in neuroimaging analysis involves mapping functional brain connections across individuals. Recent research suggests that these connections should not be viewed as fixed entities but rather dynamic aspects of brain function. However, defining a functional brain link at a group level does not necessarily mean it exists for each individual. Therefore, we must develop models that accurately reveal the existence or absence of a connection for every single participant, without relying on assumptions from a prior distribution. By applying a probabilistic framework to data from 1,200 participants without any prior assumptions, our findings indicate that functional brain connections are widespread throughout the brain and follow a principle of'shortest path'. Notably, our results show that these connections are consistently strong in areas responsible for attention, and we further demonstrate that our approach enables the accurate prediction of an individual's resting-state brain activity based on their age, gender, and cognitive ability, all while maintaining statistical reliability.

In a single-hop beeping network connecting $n$ agents, each node receives a distinct beeping signal from a central leader and uses this to establish a personal identifier. However, the current method for assigning names at a central location may lead to an efficient technique called \emph{power-saving naming}. This naming convention allows agents to create their own unique identifiers using local signals from a central leader and then share their findings with other agents through an efficient \emph{leader-coordinated initialization} process. This new approach leads to a more decentralized and efficient process, enabling name creation and initialization to be completed in a reduced number of steps, specifically $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$, and thus saving significant amounts of energy while using minimal power to achieve optimal results, specifically $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{1/2})$. This new method overperforms by achieving nearly double the number of steps required to save nearly three and a half times the amount of energy compared to a current best technique known as double-covered naming, achieving savings of around fifty percent while using fifty percent more energy than a current best technique known as sequence naming.

Recent research has successfully applied transformer models on code-mixed social media text, but using fixed positional encoding may hinder the model's ability to learn linguistic patterns, especially when dealing with diverse dialects on a single post. To overcome this limitation, our approach uses a new positional encoding method that adapts to dialects based on transition points, enabling efficient learning of code-mixed dialects. Experimental results show that our model outperforms the competition in identifying code-mixed dialects and achieves significant reductions in feature dimensionality, with a best case scenario yielding 76.91% accuracy with just 5 variables.

The superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S are analyzed as a function of pressure within a broadened one-band model that accounts for both isotopic effects and a van Hove singularity in the density of states. The model's behavior in H$_{3}$S as pressure varies is characteristic, with a critical temperature exhibiting a typical logarithmic dependence in the vicinity of a van Hove singularity, known as a Coulomb gap. The results predict that the critical temperature peaks at a pressure of approximately 155 GPa due to an unusual dependence on isotopes. This peak is attributed to a competition between the effects of pressure-induced increasing density and the effects of a van Hove singularity on superconductivity. Isotope effects are found to be benign at low and high pressures due to varying dependencies in different pressure ranges. The predicted critical temperature at 155 GPa matches the experimental value, with potential implications that surpass the predictability of single-factor models.

The conventional approach to motion planning involves navigating around physical obstacles based on perceived environment data and an chosen itinerary. However, in situations where multiple agents are interacting, other participants may intentionally create barriers to block desired paths, requiring adaptive environment perception and interpretation. This research focuses on a simplified, two-dimensional setting where a mobile agent moves on a straight line and encounters a moving point mass, which can be positioned by two integer values. By studying this "limiter" agent, we aim to develop innovative methods for limiting the limited movement areas visible to the mobile agent. We outline computational algorithms generating these restricted zones for the limiter agent and demonstrate their applications in deriving optimal navigation paths with guaranteed arrival and safety. This approach is exemplified in a game where the goal is to find the closest path to a target while avoiding obstacles, and we present computational results demonstrating the scalability of these methods.

This research introduces an efficient visual relocalization technique based on geometric information and machine learning features that can rapidly establish relationships between a device's current image and a database of pre-recorded map, all while minimizing computational time. We train a neural network to generate feature maps that can accurately localize camera perspectives. These feature maps enable cameras to track distinctive landmarks and determine their position in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, a surface feature mapping approach allows us to construct a database of features that can accurately capture camera movements in three-dimensional space and efficiently match new images with existing features, all while minimizing computational time. We tested the technique in real-time conditions by simulating outdoor scenarios and found that it successfully localized the camera's position in nearly 90% of cases with only a single image reference.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the problem of determining user choice and precoder jointly presents significant challenges. The existing approach for combining choice and precoder in a single step, although highly effective, suffers from notable drawbacks. The objective of this research is to devise an alternative method that mitigates the adverse effects of 'choice noise' while maintaining precision in precoder estimation. The proposed solution entails two stages - first, estimating precoders alone using a regularization technique called Group LASSO, and then selecting users based on a metric that minimizes noise and streamlines computation. The proposed method boasts superior performance in MIMO performance metrics. The efficacy and advantages of this approach are exemplified through simulations conducted under various MIMO scenarios.

We prove that the group of unitary transformations of an arrangement of tropical vectors in multiple dimensions has a subset that shares similar properties to a fundamental group, and this subset can be expressed as the inverse image of a degree-based function, where functions of this nature have a specific structural component when composed with line mappings in the algebraic sense, which ultimately implies the existence of a subset that induces an isomorphism upon intersection, resulting in the equivalence of certain divisor classes, which is an intermediate step in demonstrating that the quotient of two tropical semifields is finitely generated if and only if the quotient with an additional arbitrary field element is finitely generated, which is then leveraged to prove that for any given tropical semifield, the quotient of two tropical semifields results in another semifield that is finitely generated over the original semifield, with the added requirement that it satisfies specific homomorphism conditions with respect to a field containing the coefficients of the tropical functions.

A significant area of study within the analysis of stochastic processes involves identifying mechanisms through which a process's characteristics can be related to those of a different process. Determining the conditions under which such relationships can be established and the accuracy of the resulting approximations is a key focus. This work builds upon existing research in this domain by establishing a method for determining the conditions under which a process's residuals converge to a normal distribution. The process relies on a different approach from those used in existing works, which are centered on the concept of local time. Instead, we adopt a method involving evaluation at random times, which is facilitated by the integration of Poisson random measures to create random time variables. The method also allows us to generalize a different type of relationship, namely that between random times and the process itself, under specific conditions. As a result, we are able to derive consistent convergence to a Q-process. As an application of these findings, we are able to provide a different interpretation of the relationships between local times and the process itself, specifically in the context of a different type of Markov process, namely a BES(0) process, which is equivalent to a Brownian motion under a different time measure.

Building on Fox's biquadratic invariant, which he calculated through the componennt formal group, we show that its expansion, the Fox-Hartenstein invariant, results in a three-order characteristic of Vassiliev invariants. Notably, the Vassiliev invariant, in the field of rational numbers, does not equal zero, whereas the Fox-Hartenstein invariant does when the field is real. Additionally, we establish a relation between this new invariant and the LP invariant. Furthermore, we utilize cohomology of braid groups to formulate a multiplicative modification of the LP invariant, which holds the property of being Vassiliev of the third order. Alongside this, we find that the LP invariant displays an inverse relationship with the Fox-Hartenstein invariant and that their compositions conform to a specific trace equation. Alongside these findings, we also prove that the LP invariant, when the field is rational, does not satisfy a specific homomorphism equation yet satisfies it when the field is real.

Even though certain iron-based superconductors exhibit spin and orbital orderings, the iron-based superconductor LiFeAs remains stable under extreme pressure and has unique properties that set it apart from other iron-based compounds, making the study of its orbital ordering and its relationship with superconductivity all the more compelling. In this study, we used x-ray diffraction to analyze LiFeAs at various temperatures and pressures, examining the orbital ordering's impact on its structure. LiFeAs's lattice shows no change upon cooling below its superconducting critical temperature of 18 Kelvin, regardless of whether it's under high pressure or not. In contrast, similar experiments on LiFeAs under extreme pressure and in the presence of magnetic field did not yield any observable nematic deformation. These findings suggest that, unlike other iron-based compounds, LiFeAs does not exhibit orbital ordering or nematicity. As a result, LiFeAs's unconventional superconductivity may have an entirely different origin, potentially linking it to its unique properties without requiring orbital ordering.

This research presents a comprehensive global analysis of the two-Higgs doublet model in light of contemporary and impending experimental findings, taking into account the latest results from the LHC and top quark feed-down to the bottom sector. Our findings emphasize the significance of non-production mechanisms in determining the properties of the second Higgs boson. We have also considered the impact of incorporating neutrino sectors to the model, and in doing so, we have identified parameter regions that can explain neutrino's small mass and mixing, known as the neutrino origin of the two-Higgs doublet model. Furthermore, our predictions for various observable quantities, such as Higgs branching ratios and couplings, are determined solely based on experimental data. Finally, we have assessed the capabilities of forthcoming experiments including the High-Luminosity LHC and the proton-proton collider.

We suggest that utilizing a neuroevolutionary approach can effectively train particles to exhibit self-assembly behaviors, where the targets for this study are complex three-dimensional objects. To explore this possibility, we have successfully implemented a new self-assembly model where the goals are undefined and unexplored in the context of complex 3D shapes, where real-world frameworks are used for comparison. Furthermore, we have discovered that employing existing frameworks does not necessarily lead to desirable results, as these frameworks can limit the potential of our model. We have also identified several characteristics of successful self-assembly systems, where the targets for this study are complex 3D objects. Lastly, we have discussed the potential implications of our findings, where the targets for this study are real-world images, and several potential applications have been examined.

I'm examining the chiral gauge theory with the Wilson action, focusing on its robust characteristics in both 2D and 4D and its application to partial chiral models such as QCD. In 2D, one aspect of the theory's baryonic spectrum relates to a generalized chiral symmetry. In 4D, baryon states arise from the edge of a Néel-valence-bond phase inspired by lattice constructions, also linked to a generalized chiral symmetry that emerges when the external gauge field reaches a critical strength. Additionally, we find that if the phases mentioned are not present, the edge mode remains even when the external gauge field reaches zero, displaying a chemical potential-induced chiral symmetry breaking unique to partial chiral gauge theories.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the steady Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we explore the relationship between input forces and resulting flow patterns in dimension 3 or higher. This work shows that the steady Navier-Stokes equation becomes unstable when certain flow patterns are considered, resulting in the equation being classified as poorly defined in certain mathematical frameworks. Conversely, we found that the steady equation remains stable when these specific flow patterns are absent, utilizing specific mathematical frameworks known as Besov spaces.

In antiferromagnetic insulators, a notable change occurs when they are heated, resulting in a shift along the spectral axis accompanied by a characteristic broadening of the magnon line, which can be described using a specific theoretical framework analogous to the Schwinger boson approach. The shape of the magnon line follows a Lorentzian pattern at higher temperatures or when coupling strength is pronounced, whereas it aligns closer to a Gaussian shape at lower temperatures and weaker coupling strengths. The research demonstrates that the width of the magnon line is influenced more significantly by temperature than it is by doping, which suggests that this method could be used to detect any remaining residual correlations within doped compounds that have transitioned into a state known as a normal metal. The study provides an analytical solution for one-dimensional systems and approximates the behavior of two-dimensional systems for sufficiently high temperatures or weak coupling strengths of the spin interaction.

This research introduces two modifications to enhance the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, specifically involving a modified decoding algorithm and a key mixing procedure. Firstly, we propose introducing a key mixing step after the matrix decomposition step in the traditional Loidreau scheme to thwart linear attacks. Secondly, we suggest employing a standard binary matrix instead of the Goppa code for key generation, followed by a Gaussian elimination decoding method. Experimental analysis of the modified system utilizing Goppa codes of various degrees reveals they offer comparable or even superior computational performance and security compared to the original scheme.

To enhance the ability of a language model to generalize to specific words, additional information about word meanings can be incorporated into the model. This can be done by including dictionaries, such as Wiktionary, which provide definitions and broader word categories. An examination discovered that conventional self-supervised learning methods used in models like BERT overlook crucial aspects of word usage when learning word meanings. An innovative approach, referred to as Dict-BERT, was proposed to effectively utilize dictionaries in pre-trained language models. An experiment demonstrated the benefits of including definitions in word embeddings, revealing significant enhancements in word similarity assessment and sentence semantic relatedness detection. Additionally, Dict-BERT yielded superior performance on sentence classification tasks.

We analyze the structure of the minimal spanning acycles on a minimal spanning tree, focusing on a uniformly random minimal spanning tree of a complete graph of n points. It's observed that for a large subset of these trees, the acycles will have no cycles of size less than k, where the probability decreases exponentially with n. This leads to the conclusion that for almost all such trees, the number of connected components in the persistence diagram generated by the tree will be at most log(n). We extend this to uniformly random minimal spanning acycles of an n-point simplicial complex, obtained from the uniform minimal spanning trees sequence. Using a similar approach, it's shown that for almost all such acycles, the number of connected components in the persistence diagram will be at most log(n).

By enabling the joint modeling of data owned by multiple parties without direct data exchanges, Federated Learning offers improved privacy and security. However, this concept was recently compromised with the introduction of pragmatic privacy attacks that utilize gradient exchange data to reconstruct sensitive information. These attacks challenge the assumptions made about the data distribution in Vertical FL and facilitate successful knowledge extraction from multiple parties. Furthermore, simulation results indicate that such attacks can be more effective than traditional privacy assaults. In response to these threats, methods to detect and prevent pragmatic privacy assaults are being actively explored.

A novel theoretical approach called B-Mesogenesis has been proposed, suggesting that certain types of particles called dark matter may exist. According to this theory, a type of dark matter particle can be formed when a B-meson decays into a proton and another particle called a dark antibaryon. Research has shown that such decays are feasible and can be studied further, potentially leading to a breakthrough in understanding dark matter. A mathematical method for determining the probability of this decay process has been established, allowing scientists to study it. Analysis indicates that although the probability of this decay is small, it may be detectable at particle accelerators like the FCC and future HEP facilities. A related mode of decay involving dark matter is also possible for other particles called charmed mesons.

The growing prominence of intelligent, interconnected systems within modern cities is forcing a reckoning: can these powerful networks truly enhance our safety, or do they instead create devastating vulnerabilities?  Urban defense systems are being tested by a new threat - the SOCIO-CPA, a style of attack that targets the intricate web of physical, cyber, and social infrastructure underlying these cities. In response to this danger, a innovative game model and simulation have been created for simulating city managers' strategic decision-making processes during extended periods of assault. This approach involves converting complex defense problems into manageable game-theoretic formats, allowing analysis and resolution of critical challenges in managing resources, coordinating efforts, and allocating resources across multiple assault phases. In a virtual environment, the interactive nature of this game model enables different city protocol developers and attackers to engage in counter-initiatives and counter-campaigns, promoting further exploration and experimentation of various tactics and methods.

Black holes transition into one another through the Hawking-Page phase shift. A specific black hole $T_{\infty}$ is formed when certain conditions are applied to the Schwarzschild, charged Schwarzschild, and Schwarzschild-(anti)-de Sitter metrics in an imaginary chamber. These phase transitions occur in the thermodynamic equilibrium state at constant temperature, and the critical points of each Hawking-Page phase shift curve dictate the duration of each phase shift process. The thermal behavior of these phase shifts was previously assessed; however, this study reveals that the thermal radiation of large black holes is temporary, extinguished by the temperature reaching zero. Hawking-Page phase shifts do not occur in imaginary chambers containing imaginary black holes and negative imaginary chambers containing pseudo-black holes.

Document ranking tasks are significantly hindered by label noise, causing issues in practical applications. Existing approaches either rely on precise annotations or employ regressive methods with inherent flaws, as their predictions are heavily influenced by noisy initial labels. We present a novel method that mitigates label noise by utilizing a collaborative ranking process and proposing the cluster-wise label noise ranking (CLNR) method. CLNR involves selecting and ranking documents in batches using a specific sampling strategy, and subsequently calculates the probability of each document's correct label through Bayesian inference. We minimize the difference between the predicted probabilities and the actual ground-truth labels, treating it as a maximum likelihood problem while addressing the label noise. Experiments on various datasets show that our proposed method outperforms existing methods, achieving a 12% improvement in ranking accuracy.

The exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in various applications has driven their widespread adoption, yet many current studies assume a vast amount of node labels are available. In reality, labels are often scarce and expensive to obtain. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative pseudo-labeling approach called Multi-spectral Pseudo-labeling for GNNs (Multi-P2L). By leveraging the strengths of both spectral and spatial features, our method simultaneously produces pseudo-labels and refines the GNN model in an end-to-end trainable manner, providing better representation learning. We conduct comprehensive experiments on six real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, outperforming existing state-of-the-art semi-supervised GNN models significantly when dealing with limited labels.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments like the AWAKE project. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection affect the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra. Specifically, the study demonstrates that plasma radial variations can produce noticeable differences in beam dynamics, while offset electron injections enable separate analysis of beam populations. This distinct analysis is possible due to the distinct pico-second timing of the electron and proton beams used in the AWAKE experiment. By applying a tight focusing technique to concentrate plasma electrons along the beam axis, the analysis becomes possible without requiring complex data processing. This work utilizes PARIS code simulations to verify the effectiveness of employing a pinched plasma focus.

This study addresses the challenge of building accurate decision trees on a dataset distributed among multiple parties, while maintaining the confidentiality of the data and ensuring that results are reliable. To achieve data confidentiality, we utilize differential privacy, and the existing methods for learning decision trees under differential privacy are either too resource-intensive or too limited in scope. In response, we've developed novel algorithms that coordinate the creation of decision trees across multiple parties in a way that allows us to gauge their precision. These new methods incorporate the concept of federated learning, and they effectively solve the problem of learning decision trees under differential privacy in a distributed environment. To validate the accuracy of our methods, we tested them on synthetic and real-world datasets and demonstrated to a statistical certainty that the resulting tree predictions are trustworthy. Furthermore, we applied our methods to actual datasets, and the results showed that they effectively maintain the confidentiality of the data while yielding trees that are capable of achieving an accuracy of up to 96% without needing the entire dataset.

We introduce a novel variational method for computing representations of probability measures that minimize a specified R\'enyi divergence while adhering to constraints such as probability conservation and non-negativity. The approach is versatile, applicable to a range of divergences, including Kullback-Leibler and Wasserstein divergences, at any order. The method's convergence rate is analyzed and empirical evaluations demonstrate the benefits of our regularization scheme, particularly in the presence of sparse data.

This paper introduces a new approach for model selection in chain event graphs through a Bayesian maximum a posteriori framework. This methodology automatically identifies the number of nodes in each partition and determines the probability of transitioning between them. Its efficient Bayesian framework makes it feasible to analyze intricate networks that other methods struggle to handle. We've developed a computationally rapid realignment algorithm that enables the integration of different models into a single framework, allowing for the examination of a wide range of models and the evaluation of their goodness of fit. The proposed approach is demonstrated through analysis of two real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to produce reliable parameter estimates and identifying models that effectively explain observed data.

In a Hilbert space, we're working with the problem of minimizing a convex functional, and we've developed a new method involving Damped Inertial Mechanics with vanishing Tikhonov regularization. When we take the limit of this functional as it approaches 0, we've shown both theoretically and numerically that it converges strongly toward the minimal norm solution under the condition that the functional has a finite gamma-Lipschitz constant. When this condition isn't met, we've established that the convergence rate is influenced by the angle between the gradient of the functional and the normal vector of its subdifferential. A numerical example demonstrating convergence even when the functional isn't globally Lipschitz is provided.

This research explores the dynamics of a simplified robot model operating on a surface with periodic texture patterns. The robot's movement is constrained by a threshold limit on its perception radius. When the texture patterns are evenly spaced and the robot's starting position falls within a specific range, it will eventually come to rest at a consistent position. However, when the robot's perception limit exceeds a certain threshold, its behavior becomes more unpredictable, and further changes in the parameter values can cause the robot to fluctuate between different resting states in an irregular manner. Furthermore, altering the texture pattern by introducing asymmetries can also lead to the robot exhibiting these unstable and erratic movements.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, where strong Coulomb repulsion exists, our research involves computing the complex microwave conductivity of superconductors containing extended defects. Through computer simulations, we investigated how microwave conductivity changes at extremely low temperatures and also analyzed how it's influenced by changes in electron doping and energy within the microwave frequency range. We discovered that Coulomb repulsion, in contrast to conventional superconductors, does not impede the occurrence of superconductivity. Instead, it plays a crucial role in determining the transition temperature and superconducting gap values. Moreover, our findings indicate that power-dependent behavior in microwave conductivity is significantly influenced by both Coulomb repulsion and density of states peaks, resulting in distinct resonance structures. We observed that Coulomb repulsion, in this case, enhances the amplitude of these resonance structures compared to conventional superconductors.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this specific type of flow is provided, focusing primarily on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

A computer generates an animated plant growth sequence from a starting plant configuration. Plant growth is a complex, non-linear process involving random events. For optimal development, a plant must balance growth against potential damage to avoid degradation. Our approach, called GrowSpace, utilizes reinforcement learning to teach plants with geometric shapes and target images of full growth. The learning process involves a policy network that selects beneficial geometric transformations, like extending stems and developing leaves, and a critic network that assesses the effectiveness of these choices. To expedite development, we introduced a novel loss function incorporating a model-based Monte Carlo tree search. Our experiments demonstrate that plants grown using this method outperform controls in diverse environments.

We outline the seed loopevil theorem, which establishes a specific convergence criterion for Schram polynomials to evaluate arbitrary seed loop aversions. We define QD aversions as the limiting case of QD insertions and demonstrate that a certain type of QD insertion scales proportionally to the conformal loop equation's solution for uniform loop aversion. Additionally, we establish a direct relationship between quantum disk correspondence and standard conformal field theory approaches to the Segal-Sugimoto model and the Wess-Zumino-Witten model. Our proof also relies on the existence of a unique conformal field theory describing the fusion product of quantum disks, which we constructed separately using conformal fusion theory based on the Verlinde formula, despite discovering an apparent anomaly in the process.

The Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI) aims to standardize data analysis workflows in the medical imaging field. One of the primary objectives of IBSI is to develop and promote normalization techniques for imaging biomarkers to enhance research reproducibility and reduce the risk of false positive conclusions due to statistical biases. This move is triggered by concerns over the limited applicability of machine learning methods in medical imaging, as well as the ongoing debate around the inaccuracies in the reporting of computational MRI research. A key paper published by Nature in 2017 highlighted the issues of incomplete data reporting in medical imaging research. In response, IBSI has developed a comprehensive checklist for standardizing data analysis workflows and promoting transparency in computing methods. A central tenet of IBSI is the collaboration with diverse research communities to ensure the successful implementation of this initiative.

The angular dependence of the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction cross-sections,
specifically their edgewise and edgeworth terms, is extensively discussed in this paper.
We first examine the unique characteristics of the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ channels'
photoproduction edgewise terms in detail, discovering that they exhibit an energy-independent
pattern below 2.5 GeV but display diversity when the edgewise terms can be directly linked
to the dominant resonance contributions. In contrast, the edgewise terms in the $K\Sigma$ channel
show a distinct behavior compared to the $K\Lambda$ channel, largely due to isospin symmetry.
We further explore this phenomenon in detail and emphasize its practical implications in resonance analysis.
We present edgewise moment solutions that can be potentially utilized in extracting resonance properties.
We also analyze the high-energy behavior of the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction edgewise terms,
establishing a direct connection between them and the dominant high-spin nucleon and delta resonance
excitations in this energy domain. We demonstrate that the latter significantly contributes to the former.
Importantly, this connection underpins the concept of "isospin symmetry in the $K$-photoproduction channels".
Furthermore, we examine the role of the $G_{18-23}$, $G_{38-43}$, and $G_{58

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset consisting of 55,134 images. The paper focuses on the dataset's preprocessing phase, outlining the specific chain of transformations applied to the data. Utilizing OpenCV 3.6.0, the entire workflow was executed on an NVIDIA V100 GPU, significantly reducing processing time. A detailed evaluation of various image scaling methods was conducted, and the advantages of using Lanczos interpolation over Nearest Neighbor and Bilinear interpolation are documented. Moreover, the impact of data normalization via division by $L_2$ norm on network behavior was investigated. A comparative assessment of different color channel ordering configurations was performed, suggesting that standard RGB ordering yields better results. Finally, the importance of removing morphological enhancements from facial data is emphasized. All code and utilities used in this study have been made publicly available on GitHub repository https://github.com/fake308/MorphiII_Eddy_V6.

We suggest that supermassive dark objects in the Universe could be giant dark holes formed before the universe cooled down, acting as massive seeds that grew into the enormous galaxies we see today.
